extracted.intended_audience: general readers of satire and critics of Mary Baker Eddy/Christian Science
extracted.subtask_description: A satirical chapter-length critique of Mary Baker Eddy, her writing, her book Science and Health, and the organization and by-laws of the Christian Science church. The text exposes perceived literary, organizational, commercial, and doctrinal faults with illustrative quotations and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship claims for Science and Health
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether Mrs. Eddy legitimately authored Science and Health; Twain lists possibilities (she did, God did, she thinks she did, she believes she wrote it under Deity's inspiration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain treats the question with irony: he enumerates '1. That she did not write Science and Health. 2. That the Deity did (or did not) write it. 3. That She thinks She wrote it. 4. That She believes She wrote it under the Deity's inspiration.' Use as criterion for evaluating authorship assertions vs. evidence; compares personal testimony to objective proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of divine status or equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of Mrs. Eddy's apparent claims to belong to the 'Holy Family' or to be 'equal with Jesus'—e.g., paragraph placing Virgin Mary, Jesus, and Mrs. Eddy in procession; quoted claim that 'she was equal with Jesus'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain highlights textual statements and reported claims (e.g., 'Mrs. Eddy has distinctly authorized the claim in her behalf that she herself was the chosen successor to and equal of Jesus'). Use such claims as a measure of doctrinal audacity or self-elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and quality of writing (English)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of Mrs. Eddy's written English: described as 'easily the most baffling and bewildering writer in the literary trade' with 'English...always and consistently confused and crippled and poor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain points to sentences that can mislead a 'hasty or careless reader' and notes need for 'thorough English scholars' among Readers. Use examples of awkward or ambiguous phrasing (quoted passages) as evidence of poor prose and to judge reliability of authorial statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyrighting and proprietary behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency to 'copyright everything'—books, by-laws, even phrasing; an inclination to secure credit and control via copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain repeatedly notes that she 'copyrights everything' and even 'copyrighted [the By-laws] in her own name.' Use frequency and scope of copyrighting as an index of proprietary, controlling, or commercial intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercialization / monetization of instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Charging high tuition for metaphysical college courses (e.g., tuition $300 for twelve lessons; extended packages to $800; discounts limited; 'Tuition for all strictly in advance').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain reproduces a full advertisement and computes implied revenues, using the pricing strategy to judge commercial motives. Consider whether instruction is presented as charity vs. revenue source; check restrictions like 'No invalids' and limited discounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating perpetual cash income and institutional permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational moves aimed at ensuring a perpetual income and preventing disappearance of the movement (e.g., chartering a college, chartering/chartering a church, copyrighting Tenets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain contrasts ephemeral 'supernaturals' of the past with Mrs. Eddy's strategy to 'organize their forces' and 'provide a fresh Bible and a sure and perpetual cash income.' Use presence of structural revenue mechanisms as a criterion for durability and commercialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized autocratic control via by-laws
rubrics_metrics.description: By-laws designed to keep ultimate authority with the Pastor Emeritus: Board cannot fill vacancies except with her approval; certain by-laws 'can neither be amended nor annulled, except by consent of Mrs. Eddy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain quotes by-law language showing that ostensibly independent bodies (Board, Trustees, First Members) are subordinate to her veto. Use these clauses to evaluate concentration of power and absence of genuine checks and balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumentalization of committees and offices (cosmetic governance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of offices and bodies (Board of Directors, Treasurer, Clerk, First Members/Sanhedrin) that have grand titles but little independent function because of Pastor's reserved authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain characterizes these bodies as 'Boards of Spectres' or 'personal property of Mrs. Eddy.' Use mismatch between title/grandeur and actual delegated power as a sign of cosmetic governance intended to legitimize autocracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of Readers and suppression of preaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers 'shall make no remarks explanatory of the Lesson-Sermon at any time during the service' and must read from Science and Health itself; no original remarks allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain frames this as a device to prevent divergent interpretations and sect-splitting. Use such gag rules as a criterion for enforced doctrinal uniformity and to gauge openness to interpretive plurality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection, vetting, and exclusivity of membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Admission rules requiring sponsors/recommendations, elections by First Members, limitations on who may apply (e.g., 'Applications of students of the Metaphysical College must be signed by the Board of Directors'), and invitation-based entry for outsiders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain reads these safeguards as both revenue- and status-based (raising desirability). Use sponsor/recommendation requirements and limited admissions as measures of exclusivity and gatekeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ceremonial pomp to convey authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonial features (Pastor Emeritus title, Clerk's 'imperative duty' to read messages, gilded messenger) that mimic monarchical or imperial forms and add gravitas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain mocks such 'tinsel vanities' as juvenile mimicry of monarchy. Evaluate whether ceremony substitutes for substantive legitimacy or fosters cult of personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short official terms to ensure subservience
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting terms of key officers (President and Readers elected for only one year) so officials remain dependent and 'subservient' to the Pastor Emeritus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain notes the deliberate short tenure as a safeguard against accumulation of independent influence. Use term lengths as an indicator of designed dependence versus institutional stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to remove clergy worldwide without due process
rubrics_metrics.description: Pastor Emeritus 'shall have the right ... to remove a Reader from this office in any Church of Christ, Scientist, both in America and in foreign nations' by letter, without charges, explanation, or trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain contrasts this with other religious hierarchies and emphasizes arbitrary, unilateral dismissal. Use presence of unilateral dismissal powers as a criterion for authoritarian personnel control and lack of accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for strong English competency among officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers must be 'good English scholars' and 'thorough English scholars'; Clerk must understand communications or resign ('If the Clerk ... shall receive a communication ... which he does not fully understand, he shall inform her ... Failing to adhere to this By-law, the Clerk must resign').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain presents this both as correction for prior embarrassing phrasing and as an insistence on linguistic conformity. Use language competency rules to assess emphasis on controlled messaging and protection from awkward disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypocrisy of 'without a creed' claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim that the Church is 'without a creed' while the By-laws include a chapter called 'Tenets' (and copyrighted), effectively constituting a creed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain highlights the contradiction: 'It is a Church “without a creed.” Still, it has one.' Use such contradictions to evaluate rhetorical positioning versus institutional reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing psychology: making access difficult to increase desirability
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate procedures that make membership appear hard to get (invitation-only, sponsors, examinations) to enhance perceived value and demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain explains the tactic: 'the best way is to make it apparently difficult for him to get it—then he is no son of Adam if that apple does not assume an interest in his eyes.' Use as criterion for manipulative recruitment strategies and social-psychological marketing of religious affiliation.
